title: Guitar Theory You Can Play
who: someone who can play a few songs on guitar but knows almost no theory.
goal: understand how the notes, scales and chords you already play are built, then use that to improvise your own phrases.

lessons.name: The 12 notes
lessons.why: Every chord and scale you'll ever play is built from just 12 notes. Learn them, and the fretboard stops being a mystery.

teach.text: Music uses seven letters: A B C D E F G. After G it starts again at A.
Those are only the letters. Between most of them is one more note. Walk up the A string one fret at a time and watch the names.
You passed 12 different notes before A came back. Two pairs have nothing between them: B and C, and E and F. Play them and notice they're only one fret apart.

examples.text: On the low E string, E is open and F is the very next fret: no note in between. Play: E:0 (E), E:1 (F)
examples.raw: On the low E string, E is open and F is the very next fret: no note in between. Play: E:0 (E), E:1 (F)

practice.text: Find: play every note without a ♯ on the A string, frets 0 to 12, in any order. → A:0 (A), A:2 (B), A:3 (C), A:5 (D), A:7 (E), A:8 (F), A:10 (G), A:12 (A)

actions.prompt: play every note without a ♯ on the A string, frets 0 to 12, in any order.

practice.raw: Find: play every note without a ♯ on the A string, frets 0 to 12, in any order. → A:0 (A), A:2 (B), A:3 (C), A:5 (D), A:7 (E), A:8 (F), A:10 (G), A:12 (A)

quiz.prompt: How many different notes are there before the names repeat?

fixes.fix: 7 is only the letters. Add the 5 in-between notes and you get 12.
8 counts the starting note twice. The 12th fret note is the same note again, higher.

quiz.prompt: On the low E string, play the note that comes right after E.

fixes.fix: There's no note between E and F, so F is just one fret up.

quiz.prompt: Which pair has no note in between?

fixes.fix: C♯ sits between C and D. Only B–C and E–F are neighbors.
F♯ sits between F and G.

lessons.remember: 12 notes: 7 letters plus 5 in-between notes. Nothing sits between B–C or E–F.

lessons.name: Half steps and whole steps
lessons.why: Every scale and chord is a pattern of two step sizes. On guitar they're simply 1 fret and 2 frets.

teach.text: A **half step** is the smallest step in music: one fret.
A **whole step** is two frets.
It works the same on every string.

examples.text: G to A is a whole step, because G♯ sits between them. Listen: G:0 (G), G:2 (A)
examples.raw: G to A is a whole step, because G♯ sits between them. Listen: G:0 (G), G:2 (A)

examples.text: B to C is a half step, because nothing sits between them. Listen: B:0 (B), B:1 (C)
examples.raw: B to C is a half step, because nothing sits between them. Listen: B:0 (B), B:1 (C)

practice.text: Find: play any two notes a whole step apart on the D string. (Pass: same string, frets 2 apart.)

actions.prompt: play any two notes a whole step apart on the D string. (Pass: same string, frets 2 apart.)

practice.raw: Find: play any two notes a whole step apart on the D string. (Pass: same string, frets 2 apart.)

practice.text: Find: play any two notes a half step apart on the G string. (Pass: same string, frets 1 apart.)

actions.prompt: play any two notes a half step apart on the G string. (Pass: same string, frets 1 apart.)

practice.raw: Find: play any two notes a half step apart on the G string. (Pass: same string, frets 1 apart.)

quiz.prompt: Start on A:5 (D). Play the note a whole step higher on the same string.

fixes.fix: That's a half step. A whole step is two frets.

quiz.prompt: E to F is a...

fixes.fix: Nothing sits between E and F, so they're one fret apart.

quiz.prompt: On any string, a whole step is...

fixes.fix: 1 fret is a half step.
Frets are evenly spaced in half steps on every string.

lessons.remember: 1 fret = half step. 2 frets = whole step.

lessons.name: Sharps and flats
lessons.why: Chord charts and songs use names like F♯ and B♭. They're just the in-between notes.

teach.text: ♯ (sharp) means one fret higher. C is A:3, so C♯ is one fret up.
♭ (flat) means one fret lower. D is A:5, so D♭ is one fret down: the same fret as C♯.
So each in-between note has two names: C♯ = D♭, D♯ = E♭, F♯ = G♭, G♯ = A♭, A♯ = B♭. Which name is used depends on the key (Module 3).

examples.text: On the low E string, fret 4 is G♯, also called A♭. Play: E:4 (G♯)
examples.raw: On the low E string, fret 4 is G♯, also called A♭. Play: E:4 (G♯)

practice.text: Find: play F♯ on the low E string. → E:2 (F♯)

actions.prompt: play F♯ on the low E string.

practice.raw: Find: play F♯ on the low E string. → E:2 (F♯)

practice.text: Find: play B♭ on the A string. → A:1 (B♭)

actions.prompt: play B♭ on the A string.

practice.raw: Find: play B♭ on the A string. → A:1 (B♭)

quiz.prompt: Another name for G♯ is...

fixes.fix: G♭ is one fret below G. G♯ is one fret above G, which is the same fret as A♭.
A♯ is one fret above A.

quiz.prompt: Play E♭ on the D string.

fixes.fix: That's E. E♭ is one fret lower.

quiz.prompt: One fret above E is...

fixes.fix: There's no note between E and F, so one fret up from E is F.

lessons.remember: ♯ = up one fret. ♭ = down one fret. One sound can have two names.

lessons.name: Open strings and finding any note
lessons.why: If you can name the open strings and count frets, you can find any note on the guitar.

teach.text: From thickest to thinnest, the open strings are **E A D G B E**. A way to remember: "Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie."
To find a note, start from the open string and count up one half step per fret. C on the A string: A, A♯, B, C.
Shortcut: fret 5 on a string is the same note as the next thinner string open. The one exception is the G string, where it's fret 4. Guitarists use this to tune.

practice.text: Find: G on the low E string. → E:3 (G)

actions.prompt: G on the low E string.

practice.raw: Find: G on the low E string. → E:3 (G)

practice.text: Find: A on the G string. → G:2 (A)

actions.prompt: A on the G string.

practice.raw: Find: A on the G string. → G:2 (A)

practice.text: Find: D on the B string. → B:3 (D)

actions.prompt: D on the B string.

practice.raw: Find: D on the B string. → B:3 (D)

quiz.prompt: Play C on the B string.

fixes.fix: From B, one fret up is C, because there's nothing between B and C.

quiz.prompt: Play A on the low E string.
The open strings from thickest to thinnest are...

options.text: E A D G B E
E B G D A E

fixes.when: E B G D A E
fixes.fix: That's thinnest to thickest.

lessons.remember: E A D G B E, then count frets up from the open string.

lessons.name: Octaves
lessons.why: The same note appears all over the neck. Octaves let you find it fast.

teach.text: Play the A string open, then fret 12. Same name, higher sound. That's an **octave**: 12 half steps.
Octaves also sit across strings. From a note on the low E or A string, go two strings thinner and two frets up.
The same shape from the A string:

practice.text: Find: play E:3 (G), then the G an octave higher using the same shape. → D:5 (G)

actions.prompt: play E:3 (G), then the G an octave higher using the same shape.

practice.raw: Find: play E:3 (G), then the G an octave higher using the same shape. → D:5 (G)

quiz.prompt: An octave is how many half steps?

fixes.fix: 8 counts letters plus the repeat. In half steps it's 12.

quiz.prompt: Play the low E string open, then the E an octave higher on the same string.
Play the octave of A:5 (D) using the two-strings-over shape.

fixes.fix: Two strings thinner (G string), two frets up (fret 7).

lessons.remember: 12 frets up = same note, an octave higher.

lessons.name: Reading chord diagrams and TAB
lessons.why: Most songs online are written as chord diagrams and TAB. Your phone guitar uses the same layout.

teach.text: A **chord diagram** shows the neck standing up: strings from thick (left) to thin (right), frets as rows. A dot is a finger, **O** means play the string open, **X** means don't play it. Here's E minor (022000). Play it one string at a time.
**TAB** uses six lines, one per string, with the **thin high e on top**. A number is the fret to play.

practice.text: Find: play this TAB, left to right. → A:3 (C), D:2 (E), G:0 (G)

actions.prompt: play this TAB, left to right.

practice.raw: Find: play this TAB, left to right. → A:3 (C), D:2 (E), G:0 (G)

quiz.prompt: In a chord diagram, X means...

fixes.fix: O means open. X means skip it.

quiz.prompt: Play this TAB: `B|--1--`
In TAB, the top line is...

fixes.fix: TAB is upside down compared with how you look at the guitar: the high e is on top.

lessons.remember: Diagrams show fingers on the neck. TAB shows frets on each string, high e on top.

lessons.name: Counting intervals
lessons.why: Every chord is a stack of intervals. Counting them is how you'll understand chords.

teach.text: An **interval** is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps (frets). From C to E on the A string is 4 frets: 4 half steps.
Count the moves, not the notes: C→C♯ (1), D (2), D♯ (3), E (4).

A few distances have names you'll use a lot:
   | Half steps | Name |
   |---|---|
   | 3 | minor 3rd |
   | 4 | major 3rd |
   | 5 | perfect 4th |
   | 7 | perfect 5th |
   | 12 | octave |

examples.text: A to C is 3 half steps (a minor 3rd). Play: A:0 (A), A:3 (C)
examples.raw: A to C is 3 half steps (a minor 3rd). Play: A:0 (A), A:3 (C)

practice.text: Find: play E:0 (E), then the note 5 half steps higher on the same string. → E:5 (A)

actions.prompt: play E:0 (E), then the note 5 half steps higher on the same string.

practice.raw: Find: play E:0 (E), then the note 5 half steps higher on the same string. → E:5 (A)

practice.text: Find: play D:0 (D), then the note 7 half steps higher on the same string. → D:7 (A)

actions.prompt: play D:0 (D), then the note 7 half steps higher on the same string.

practice.raw: Find: play D:0 (D), then the note 7 half steps higher on the same string. → D:7 (A)

quiz.prompt: How many half steps from G up to D?

fixes.fix: Count every fret: G♯, A, A♯, B, C, C♯, D. That's 7.

quiz.prompt: From A:2 (B), play the note 3 half steps higher on the A string.
C up to E is...

fixes.fix: Don't count the C you start on. Count the moves: 4.

lessons.remember: An interval is the distance between two notes, in half steps.

lessons.name: Major and minor 3rds: bright and dark
lessons.why: This one half step is the whole difference between happy and sad sounding chords.

teach.text: Play A, then C. That's 3 half steps: a **minor 3rd**.
Now play A, then C♯. That's 4 half steps: a **major 3rd**.

Play both pairs again. Which one sounds sadder? (choose: A to C / A to C♯) Most people hear the minor 3rd (A to C) as darker and the major 3rd as brighter. Any answer moves on, with that sentence shown.

examples.text: C to E is a major 3rd (4). C to E♭ is a minor 3rd (3). Listen: A:3 (C), A:7 (E), then A:3 (C), A:6 (E♭)
examples.raw: C to E is a major 3rd (4). C to E♭ is a minor 3rd (3). Listen: A:3 (C), A:7 (E), then A:3 (C), A:6 (E♭)

practice.text: Find: play a minor 3rd above E on the low E string. → E:3 (G)

actions.prompt: play a minor 3rd above E on the low E string.

practice.raw: Find: play a minor 3rd above E on the low E string. → E:3 (G)

practice.text: Find: play a major 3rd above E on the low E string. → E:4 (G♯)

actions.prompt: play a major 3rd above E on the low E string.

practice.raw: Find: play a major 3rd above E on the low E string. → E:4 (G♯)

quiz.prompt: Play a major 3rd above A on the A string.

fixes.fix: That's 3 half steps, a minor 3rd. A major 3rd is 4.

quiz.prompt: D to F is a...

fixes.fix: D♯, E, F is 3 half steps, so it's minor.

quiz.prompt: Play a minor 3rd above D on the D string.

lessons.remember: 3 half steps = minor 3rd (darker). 4 = major 3rd (brighter).

lessons.name: The 5th and power chords
lessons.why: The 5th is in almost every chord, and on its own it's the rock power chord.

teach.text: 7 half steps is a **perfect 5th**. It sounds strong and open. Play A, then E, 7 frets apart.
On guitar, the 5th is easy to grab: one string thinner, two frets up. Play them together: that's a **power chord** (A5).
Same shape, new root: G5.

practice.text: Find: play a power chord with its root on A:3 (C). → A:3 (C), D:5 (G)

actions.prompt: play a power chord with its root on A:3 (C).

practice.raw: Find: play a power chord with its root on A:3 (C). → A:3 (C), D:5 (G)

quiz.prompt: A perfect 5th is...

fixes.fix: 5 is a perfect 4th. The 5th is 7.

quiz.prompt: Play the 5th above the open low E string, using the power chord shape.
The 5th above E is...

fixes.fix: A is 5 half steps above E. B is 7.

lessons.remember: 7 half steps = perfect 5th. One string thinner, two frets up.

lessons.name: Tension and release
lessons.why: Good melodies and solos create a little tension, then release it. This is the feeling behind "landing" a phrase.

teach.text: Listen to a C chord, then B moving up to C. B is a half step below C and pulls into it.
Now B moving down to A over the same chord. It doesn't feel as finished.
Notes that aren't in the chord create tension. Moving to a chord note releases it. Over A minor (A, C, E), play D, then step down to C.

quiz.prompt: Over a C chord, which note pulls most strongly to C?

fixes.fix: G is in the C chord, so it's already stable. B is one half step below C.

quiz.prompt: Over A minor, play D, then land on a chord note right next to it.

fixes.fix: Am is A, C, E. From D, step down to C or up to E.

quiz.prompt: "Release" means...

options.text: Landing on a stable note after tension

fixes.fix: It's about which note you land on, not volume.

lessons.remember: Tension wants to move. Release is landing on a chord note.

lessons.name: The major scale pattern
lessons.why: The major scale is the ruler that chords, keys and numbers are measured with.

teach.text: A major scale is a pattern of steps: **Whole, Whole, Half, Whole, Whole, Whole, Half**. On one string you can see it. Play G major on the G string.
The two half steps were B to C (frets 4 to 5) and F♯ to G (frets 11 to 12).
C major uses only notes without sharps or flats, because its half steps land on E to F and B to C. Here it is in the open position.

practice.text: Find: play A major on the A string, starting open, using W W H W W W H. → A:0 (A), A:2 (B), A:4 (C♯), A:5 (D), A:7 (E), A:9 (F♯), A:11 (G♯), A:12 (A)

actions.prompt: play A major on the A string, starting open, using W W H W W W H.

practice.raw: Find: play A major on the A string, starting open, using W W H W W W H. → A:0 (A), A:2 (B), A:4 (C♯), A:5 (D), A:7 (E), A:9 (F♯), A:11 (G♯), A:12 (A)

quiz.prompt: The major scale pattern is...

options.text: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W

fixes.when: W H W W H W W
fixes.fix: That's the minor pattern (Module 6).

quiz.prompt: On the low E string, starting open, play the 4th note of E major.

fixes.fix: E (0), F♯ (2), G♯ (4), A (5). W, W, then a half step.

quiz.prompt: The notes of C major are...

options.text: C D E F G A B
C D E F♯ G A B

fixes.when: C D E F♯ G A B
fixes.fix: Following the pattern from C, the half steps land on E–F and B–C, so there are no sharps.

lessons.remember: Major scale = W W H W W W H.

lessons.name: Major scales from any note
lessons.why: This explains why songs in G have F♯, and why chord charts use the names they do.

teach.text: In G major (3.1), the 7th note was F♯, not F, because the pattern needs a whole step there. That's why the key of G has one sharp.
D major has two sharps. Play it on the D string.
Each letter is used once in a scale. That's why F major has B♭ (not A♯): the letter A is already used.

practice.text: Find: play the 7th note of A major on the A string. → A:11 (G♯)

actions.prompt: play the 7th note of A major on the A string.

practice.raw: Find: play the 7th note of A major on the A string. → A:11 (G♯)

quiz.prompt: The 7th note of G major is...

fixes.fix: E to the 7th note must be a whole step, which lands on F♯.

quiz.prompt: Which notes are sharp in D major?

fixes.fix: Follow the pattern to the 7th note: C♯ as well.

quiz.prompt: The 4th note of F major is...

fixes.fix: Same sound, but each letter is used once. A is already the 3rd, so it's B♭.

lessons.remember: Any note plus W W H W W W H gives its major scale. Each letter once.

lessons.name: Scale numbers
lessons.why: Numbers let you describe chords and melodies in any key at once. "1, 3, 5" is a chord in every key.

teach.text: Number the notes of a major scale 1 to 7. In C major: C=1, D=2, E=3, F=4, G=5, A=6, B=7. Number 1 is home.
The numbers move with the key. In G major, 1, 3 and 5 are G, B and D.
In C major, 1, 3 and 5 are C, E and G.

practice.text: Find: play 1, 3 and 5 of A major on the A string. → A:0 (A), A:4 (C♯), A:7 (E)

actions.prompt: play 1, 3 and 5 of A major on the A string.

practice.raw: Find: play 1, 3 and 5 of A major on the A string. → A:0 (A), A:4 (C♯), A:7 (E)

quiz.prompt: In G major, number 5 is...
Play 1, 3 and 5 of D major on the D string.
Which number is home?

fixes.fix: 7 is the last note before home. Home is 1.

lessons.remember: Numbers are positions in the scale. 1 is home.

lessons.name: What's inside a chord
lessons.why: You already play C, G and Am. Here's what's actually inside them.

teach.text: A chord is three or more notes played together. The basic chord, a **triad**, uses notes 1, 3 and 5 of a scale.
Play the open C chord one string at a time and watch the names.
Five strings, but only three names: C, E and G. That's 1, 3 and 5 of C major. The extra C and E are the same notes in a higher octave.

examples.text: G chord: play it string by string. Names: G, B, D (1, 3, 5 of G major). Play: E:3 (G), A:2 (B), D:0 (D), G:0 (G), B:0 (B), e:3 (G)
examples.raw: G chord: play it string by string. Names: G, B, D (1, 3, 5 of G major). Play: E:3 (G), A:2 (B), D:0 (D), G:0 (G), B:0 (B), e:3 (G)

practice.text: Find: play the open Am chord one string at a time. → A:0 (A), D:2 (E), G:2 (A), B:1 (C), e:0 (E)

actions.prompt: play the open Am chord one string at a time.

practice.raw: Find: play the open Am chord one string at a time. → A:0 (A), D:2 (E), G:2 (A), B:1 (C), e:0 (E)

quiz.prompt: The notes of a G major chord are...

fixes.fix: A triad skips every other note: 1, 3, 5. G, B, D.

quiz.prompt: The open C chord uses how many different note names?

fixes.fix: Five strings, but C and E repeat. Only C, E and G.

quiz.prompt: Play the three notes of a C triad on the A, D and G strings, any order.

lessons.remember: A triad is notes 1, 3 and 5. Chords repeat them across strings.

lessons.name: Major and minor: one finger apart
lessons.why: The difference between a happy and a sad chord is one note, and often one finger.

teach.text: Play E major one string at a time.
Now lift your finger off the G string: G♯ becomes G. That's E minor.
That one note is the **3rd**. E to G♯ is 4 half steps (major 3rd), so E is major. E to G is 3 (minor 3rd), so Em is minor. The root and 5th stay the same.

quiz.prompt: A, C, E is...

lessons.name: The root: the note a chord is named after
lessons.why: Knowing the root tells you where a chord "lives" and why some strings are skipped.

teach.text: The **root** is the note a chord is named after. In open chords, the lowest string you play is usually the root.
That's why the low E string has an X in C and A: skipping it keeps the root at the bottom. The lowest note of C is the C at A:3.

actions.prompt: play the root of Am.

practice.raw: Find: play the root of Am. → A:0 (A)

quiz.prompt: The lowest note of the open D chord is...

fixes.fix: The D chord starts on the open D string.

quiz.prompt: Play the root of the C chord.
Why is the low E string skipped in the C chord?

options.text: So the lowest note is the root, C
Because E isn't in a C chord

fixes.when: Because E isn't in a C chord
fixes.fix: E is in a C chord (it's the 3rd). It's skipped so C stays at the bottom.

lessons.remember: The root names the chord and usually sits at the bottom.

lessons.name: The chords that belong to a key
lessons.why: This is why certain chords sound right together in a song.

teach.text: Build a triad on every note of C major, using only C major notes. You get C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and B diminished. The pattern for every major key: **I ii iii IV V vi vii°** (uppercase = major, lowercase = minor).
Play the roots up the A string.
Now hear them as chords.

quiz.prompt: Which chord belongs to C major?

fixes.fix: D major needs F♯, which isn't in C major. D minor (D, F, A) fits.

quiz.prompt: In G major (G A B C D E F♯), chord vi is...

fixes.fix: vi is lowercase, so minor: E, G, B.

quiz.prompt: Play the root of chord IV in C major on the A string.

lessons.remember: Every major key: I ii iii IV V vi vii°.

lessons.name: What a key is
lessons.why: Knowing the key tells you which chords and notes will fit a song.

teach.text: A **key** is a scale plus the chords built from it, with one home. In C major, home is the note C and the C chord.
Now C, F, G and stop. It sounds like it's waiting to go home.

The first chord of the song

fixes.when: The first chord of the song
fixes.fix: Songs often start at home, but the key is about which chord feels like home.

quiz.prompt: In G major, the home chord is...

fixes.fix: D is chord V. It pulls back toward G.

quiz.prompt: Which group belongs to G major?

fixes.fix: E major needs G♯, which isn't in G major.

lessons.remember: A key is a scale plus its chords, with one home.

lessons.name: Chord numbers and common progressions
lessons.why: Thousands of songs use the same few progressions. Numbers let you play them in any key.

teach.text: Chords are named by their position in the key. In G major, I–IV–V is G, C, D. Play the roots.
Same numbers in A major: A, D, E.
I–V–vi–IV is in a huge number of pop songs. In C: C, G, Am, F.

practice.text: Find: play the roots of I–V–vi–IV in C. → A:3 (C), E:3 (G), A:0 (A), E:1 (F)

actions.prompt: play the roots of I–V–vi–IV in C.

practice.raw: Find: play the roots of I–V–vi–IV in C. → A:3 (C), E:3 (G), A:0 (A), E:1 (F)

quiz.prompt: "IV" means...

options.text: The chord built on the 4th note of the key

fixes.fix: It's about position in the key, not order in the song.

quiz.prompt: I–IV–V in A major is...

fixes.fix: Take notes 1, 4 and 5 of A major: A, D, E.

quiz.prompt: Play the root of chord V in G major on the A string.

lessons.remember: Numbers make progressions portable. I–IV–V and I–V–vi–IV are everywhere.

lessons.name: Finding the key of a song
lessons.why: Once you know a song's key, you know which scale to solo with.

teach.text: Use two clues. First: which chord feels like home? Usually the one the song ends on or keeps returning to.
Second: which key contains all the chords? G, C, D and Em are I, IV, V and vi of G major.

practice.raw: Listen: D, G, A, Bm, D strummed. Find: play the home note of this progression. → accept note D

quiz.prompt: A song uses G, C, D and Em and ends on G. Key?

fixes.fix: The D chord needs F♯, which isn't in C major.

quiz.prompt: A song uses C, F, G and Am and ends on C. Key?

fixes.fix: Every chord fits C major, and C is home.

quiz.prompt: A song uses D, G, A and Bm and ends on D. Key?

fixes.fix: These are I, IV, V and vi of D major.

lessons.remember: Find home by ear, then check which key holds every chord.

lessons.name: The relative minor
lessons.why: A minor and C major share every note. That's why the A minor pentatonic box also works in C major songs.

teach.text: Play the C major notes, but start and end on A. That's **A natural minor**.
Same notes as C major, different home. Over an Am chord, it sounds darker.
Every major key has a **relative minor**, starting on its 6th note. C major's 6th note is A.

practice.text: Find: play the home note of G major's relative minor. → accept note E

actions.prompt: play the home note of G major's relative minor.

practice.raw: Find: play the home note of G major's relative minor. → accept note E

quiz.prompt: Do C major and A minor use the same notes?

fixes.fix: A minor is C major started from A. Same notes, different home.

quiz.prompt: The relative minor of G major is...

fixes.fix: Take the 6th note of G major: E.

quiz.prompt: The relative minor of D major is...

fixes.fix: The 6th note of D major is B.

lessons.remember: Same notes, different home. The relative minor starts on the 6th note.

lessons.name: The natural minor pattern
lessons.why: The minor pattern explains why minor scales sound darker: the 3rd, 6th and 7th notes are lower.

teach.text: The natural minor pattern is **W H W W H W W**. You played it on the A string in 6.1.
Compare A major and A minor on the A string. Three notes drop a half step: the 3rd (C♯ to C), 6th (F♯ to F) and 7th (G♯ to G).

practice.text: Find: play E natural minor on the low E string, starting open. → E:0 (E), E:2 (F♯), E:3 (G), E:5 (A), E:7 (B), E:8 (C), E:10 (D), E:12 (E)

actions.prompt: play E natural minor on the low E string, starting open.

practice.raw: Find: play E natural minor on the low E string, starting open. → E:0 (E), E:2 (F♯), E:3 (G), E:5 (A), E:7 (B), E:8 (C), E:10 (D), E:12 (E)

quiz.prompt: The 3rd note of A natural minor is...

fixes.fix: C♯ is from A major. Minor has the lower 3rd, C.

quiz.prompt: Play the 3rd note of D natural minor on the D string.

fixes.fix: That's F♯, the major 3rd. Minor is one fret lower.

quiz.prompt: In natural minor, the step between notes 2 and 3 is...

fixes.fix: W H W W H W W: the second step is H.

lessons.remember: Natural minor = W H W W H W W.

lessons.name: Chords in a minor key
lessons.why: Am, F and G is one of the most common rock progressions, and it's the backing you'll improvise over in Module 9.

teach.text: Build triads on A natural minor: Am, B diminished, C, Dm, Em, F, G. The pattern for every minor key: **i ii° III iv v VI VII**.
Am, F, G is **i, VI, VII**. Play the roots on the low E string.

practice.text: Find: play the root of chord iv in A minor on the A string. → A:5 (D)

actions.prompt: play the root of chord iv in A minor on the A string.

practice.raw: Find: play the root of chord iv in A minor on the A string. → A:5 (D)

quiz.prompt: In A minor, chord i is...

fixes.fix: Lowercase i means minor. A minor's home chord is Am.

quiz.prompt: In A minor, chord VI is...

fixes.fix: The 6th note of A minor is F, and VI is major.

quiz.prompt: Am, F, G is...

fixes.fix: F is the 6th note of A minor and G is the 7th.

lessons.remember: Minor keys: i ii° III iv v VI VII. Am–F–G = i–VI–VII.

lessons.name: Beats and bars
lessons.why: Playing in time matters more than playing the right note. Every phrase lives inside a bar.

teach.text: The **beat** is the pulse you tap your foot to. In **4/4**, a **bar** has 4 beats. Beat 1 is the strongest.
Tap along on the open A string, once per beat, for two bars.

actions.prompt: A:0 (A), 8 taps, one per beat at 80 bpm (pass: each tap within 150 ms of the beat)

quiz.prompt: In 4/4, how many beats are in a bar?

fixes.fix: "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" has 8 words but only 4 beats.

quiz.prompt: The top number in 4/4 tells you...

options.text: How many beats are in a bar

fixes.fix: Speed is set by the tempo (bpm).

lessons.remember: 4/4 = four beats per bar. Beat 1 is strongest.

lessons.name: Note lengths and rests
lessons.why: How long you hold a note, and when you stay silent, shapes how a phrase feels.

teach.text: In 4/4: a **whole note** lasts 4 beats, a **half note** 2, a **quarter note** 1, and an **eighth note** half a beat. A **rest** is a timed silence.
Tap half notes: on beats 1 and 3 only, for two bars.

actions.prompt: D:7 (A), 4 taps on beats 1 and 3 (pass: within 150 ms)

quiz.prompt: A half note lasts...

fixes.fix: A half note is half of a 4-beat bar: 2 beats.

quiz.prompt: How many eighth notes fit in one bar of 4/4?

fixes.fix: Two per beat, four beats: 8.

quiz.prompt: A bar has a half note and a quarter note. How many beats are left?

fixes.fix: 2 + 1 = 3 beats used, so 1 is left.

lessons.remember: Whole 4, half 2, quarter 1, eighth ½. Rests are timed silence.

lessons.name: Off the beat
lessons.why: Starting notes between the beats is what makes riffs and solos feel alive.

teach.text: Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and". Numbers are **on the beat**. "Ands" are **off the beat**. Stressing off-beats is **syncopation**.
Tap only on the "ands" for one bar.

actions.prompt: B:5 (E), 4 taps halfway between the clicks (pass: within 120 ms)

quiz.prompt: Which is off the beat?

fixes.fix: Numbers are on the beat. Only the "ands" are off.

quiz.prompt: A note starts on the "and" of 4 and rings into the next bar. That's...

fixes.fix: Pushing a note across the strong beat is a common, deliberate feel.

lessons.remember: Numbers are on the beat. "Ands" are off the beat.

lessons.name: From seven notes to five
lessons.why: The pentatonic is the most-used soloing scale in rock and blues. Now you'll know why it works.

teach.text: Start from A natural minor (A B C D E F G) and remove notes 2 and ♭6 (B and F). You get **A C D E G**: the A minor pentatonic.
Removing B and F removes every half step. With no notes one fret apart, it's very hard to hit a note that clashes.

practice.text: Find: play E minor pentatonic on the low E string, starting open. → E:0 (E), E:3 (G), E:5 (A), E:7 (B), E:10 (D), E:12 (E)

actions.prompt: play E minor pentatonic on the low E string, starting open.

practice.raw: Find: play E minor pentatonic on the low E string, starting open. → E:0 (E), E:3 (G), E:5 (A), E:7 (B), E:10 (D), E:12 (E)

quiz.prompt: The notes of A minor pentatonic are...

fixes.fix: That's the first five notes of the minor scale. The pentatonic removes B and F instead.

quiz.prompt: Which two notes of A natural minor are removed?

fixes.fix: C and G stay. B (2) and F (♭6) go.

quiz.prompt: On the A string, play the A minor pentatonic note between E and the next A.

lessons.remember: Minor pentatonic = natural minor without 2 and ♭6.

lessons.name: Box 1 on the guitar
lessons.why: This is the shape most guitarists learn first. Now you'll know which notes are in it.

teach.text: Box 1 of A minor pentatonic sits at frets 5 to 8. It starts on A, because A is at fret 5 on the low E string. Play it from low to high.
The home notes (A) are at three places in the box.
The shape is movable. Start it on G (low E fret 3) and it becomes G minor pentatonic.

practice.text: Find: play every C in the box. → E:8 (C), G:5 (C), e:8 (C)

actions.prompt: play every C in the box.

practice.raw: Find: play every C in the box. → E:8 (C), G:5 (C), e:8 (C)

quiz.prompt: Why does box 1 of A minor pentatonic start at fret 5?

options.text: A is at fret 5 on the low E string

fixes.fix: The box starts wherever the home note is on the low E string.

quiz.prompt: Box 1 of G minor pentatonic starts at...

fixes.fix: G is at fret 3 on the low E string.

quiz.prompt: Play the highest C in box 1.

lessons.remember: Box 1 starts on the home note on the low E string.

lessons.name: The major pentatonic
lessons.why: The same box can sound happy or sad, depending on the chord under it.

teach.text: The **major pentatonic** is the major scale without notes 4 and 7. C major without F and B gives **C D E G A**: the same notes as A minor pentatonic.
Over a C chord, C feels like home. Over Am, A does.

practice.text: Find: play the box note that feels like home over a C chord, on the G string. → G:5 (C)

actions.prompt: play the box note that feels like home over a C chord, on the G string.

practice.raw: Find: play the box note that feels like home over a C chord, on the G string. → G:5 (C)

quiz.prompt: Do C major pentatonic and A minor pentatonic share the same notes?

fixes.fix: C D E G A and A C D E G are the same five notes.

quiz.prompt: G major pentatonic is...

fixes.fix: Remove notes 4 (C) and 7 (F♯) from G major.

quiz.prompt: Which minor pentatonic has the same notes as G major pentatonic?

fixes.fix: E is G major's relative minor.

lessons.remember: Same five notes, different home, depending on the chord.

lessons.name: The blue note
lessons.why: One extra note gives the pentatonic its bluesy edge.

teach.text: The **blue note** is ♭5: in A, it's **E♭**, between D and E. In box 1 it's at A:6 and G:8.
It's very tense, so pass through it and don't stop on it. On the higher strings: D, E♭, then land on E.

quiz.prompt: The blue note in E minor pentatonic is...

fixes.fix: The blue note is ♭5: 6 half steps above E is B♭.

quiz.prompt: The blue note works best as...

options.text: The last note of a phrase

fixes.when: The last note of a phrase
fixes.fix: It's very tense. Pass through it and land on a stable note.

quiz.prompt: Play the blue note on the A string in box 1.

lessons.remember: The blue note is ♭5. Pass through it, don't stop on it.

modules.title: Improvising
modules.intro: You've learned the theory. Now you'll use it, playing over a backing track.

lessons.name: Aim for the chord
lessons.why: This is the step from running the scale to soloing: aim at the notes of the chord that's playing.

teach.text: As the backing plays, the glowing notes change every bar. They're the notes of the chord playing right now.
Play anything you like from the box, but end each bar on a glowing note.

practice.text: Play along for one loop. Pass: the last note in each bar is a chord note for that bar.

actions.prompt: - Play along for one loop. Pass: the last note in each bar is a chord note for that bar.

practice.raw: Play along for one loop. Pass: the last note in each bar is a chord note for that bar.

quiz.prompt: Over F, which box notes are chord notes?

fixes.fix: F is F, A, C. In the box you have A and C.

quiz.prompt: Over G, which box notes are chord notes?

fixes.fix: G is G, B, D. In the box you have G and D.

lessons.remember: Aim for the chord, not just the scale.

lessons.name: Passing notes and landing
lessons.why: Phrases sound finished when they land well.

teach.text: Notes that aren't chord notes are fine in the middle of a phrase. They lead into chord notes.
Over the last Am bar, ending on A sounds finished. Ending on D sounds like it wants to keep going.

practice.text: Play bar 4 (Am) and end on A. → accept note A as the last note of bar 4

actions.prompt: Play bar 4 (Am) and end on A. → accept note A as the last note of bar 4

practice.raw: Play bar 4 (Am) and end on A. → accept note A as the last note of bar 4

quiz.prompt: Which ending sounds most finished over the last Am bar?

fixes.fix: D isn't in Am. A is the home note.

lessons.remember: Pass through tension, land on a chord note.

lessons.name: One idea, four bars
lessons.why: Good solos often say one idea, repeat it, change it, then finish.

teach.text: Play a short idea (3 or 4 notes) in bar 1. The app records it.
Then choose what happens next: **Repeat it**, **Change the rhythm**, or **Answer it** (turn the shape around and land on a chord note). These are the builder moves.

Finish bar 4 on A.
   - Listen (example): bar 1 B:5 (E), B:8 (G), e:5 (A); bar 2 the same; bar 3 e:5 (A), B:8 (G), G:7 (D); bar 4 B:8 (G), B:5 (E), B:8 (G), e:5 (A)

practice.text: Build four bars from your own idea. Pass: two bars share the same idea, and bar 4 ends on A.

actions.prompt: Build four bars from your own idea. Pass: two bars share the same idea, and bar 4 ends on A.

practice.raw: Build four bars from your own idea. Pass: two bars share the same idea, and bar 4 ends on A.

lessons.remember: One idea, said again, changed, then finished.

lessons.name: Rhythm and space
lessons.why: Silence and off-beat notes make a phrase sound like music, not an exercise.

teach.text: Leave a gap. A rest lets the listener hear your idea.
Start one note on an "and" (off the beat).

practice.text: Play one loop with at least one rest inside a bar and one note starting off the beat.

actions.prompt: Play one loop with at least one rest inside a bar and one note starting off the beat.

practice.raw: Play one loop with at least one rest inside a bar and one note starting off the beat.

lessons.remember: Where a note lands matters as much as which note it is.

lessons.name: The blue note in a phrase

teach.text: Add E♭ (G:8 or A:6) once, passing from D to E.

practice.text: Play one loop using E♭ once. Pass: E♭ is followed straight away by D or E, and never ends a bar.

actions.prompt: Play one loop using E♭ once. Pass: E♭ is followed straight away by D or E, and never ends a bar.

practice.raw: Play one loop using E♭ once. Pass: E♭ is followed straight away by D or E, and never ends a bar.

lessons.remember: The blue note is a stepping stone.

lessons.name: Final challenge: four bars, no help

goals: Every bar ends on a chord note for that bar.
At least two bars share the same idea.
At least one rest inside a bar.
At most one scale run (three or more notes stepping through the box in one direction).

modules.title: What comes next
items: **Listening mode:** play your real guitar and the app hears it.
The other four pentatonic boxes, and the CAGED system for linking shapes across the neck.
Modes as colors: Dorian and Mixolydian.
